view: Mentioning the two men's entry into prison implies the preceding, unstated imprisonment of Joseph.
The word marks a new shared companionship: the two entered prison in Joseph's company, at the same time as he did.
note: Others say the wording does not fix when each was admitted.

view: The two could have entered before, after, or together with Joseph; the wording establishes their shared prison company or room without fixing simultaneous admission.
note: This differs from the claim that maʿa requires simultaneous entry.

view: Placing 'with him' before 'prison' emphasizes companionship; the phrase may also soften the account of imprisonment on seeing Joseph or describe his imprisonment without denying his choice.
The object precedes the subject for emphasis, and 'one of them said' answers an implicit narrative question after the unstated 'they imprisoned him.'
Al-sijn here means the place of confinement, as required by entering it; its kasra vowel distinguishes this from the act of imprisonment.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr says all readers use kasra here.

view: Fityān is the dual of fatā, a weak-y noun; the form al-futu is irregular.
Fatā may mean a young man or an enslaved male servant of any age; a female servant is fatāt. The two may have been young or old.
note: Some extend the term to a free servant as well.

view: They are called young men because neither surpassed the other in making a claim and each referred the matter to his companion.
The two prisoners served Egypt's king: one tended his food as baker or steward, and the other his drink as cupbearer or wine server.
note: Some specify enslavement; Asad attributes the occupations to the Bible while noting that the Qur'an leaves the offences unstated.

view: The Qur'an itself leaves the prisoners' identities unspecified; the baker and cupbearer identification comes from reports or the Torah.
One account names the king al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid and the servants Mujlith or Majlath and Nabu or Nabwa, with Nabu serving wine.
note: The names and king's patronymic differ across reports.

view: Other accounts name the servants Sharham Aqam and Sharham Asham, or Sharham and Sarham; another names the cupbearer Manja and baker Majlath.
note: These names compete with the Mujlith and Nabu account.

view: The king jailed the baker or food steward on suspicion of trying to poison him and the cupbearer on suspicion of complicity or collusion.
note: The reports vary on whether the cupbearer agreed, was merely suspected, or withdrew.

view: Conspirators bribed both servants to poison the king; the cupbearer withdrew and warned him, but the baker poisoned the food. An animal test exposed the poisoned food, and both were jailed.
note: One version has the baker warn against drinking; another says they accused each other; one gives a year in prison.

view: The prisoners were jailed when the king became angry; their offences are unspecified in the Qur'an.
Joseph was paraded in chains on a donkey for defying his mistress, and said this punishment was easier than Hell.
Joseph cared for sick or wounded prisoners, comforted the grieving, made room for cramped inmates, and sought or collected aid for the needy.
note: Some add intercession, borrowing for the needy, truthful speech, or exhortation to good.

view: Joseph worshipped God in prison, including prayer, fasting, and night devotion; his obedience, tears, and piety helped win the inmates' trust and affection.
Joseph urged despairing prisoners to be patient, promising reward, purification, and relief; they admired his speech, conduct, and comforting presence.
Joseph introduced himself as descended from Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham; the keeper promised him the best confinement or his choice of quarters, though he could not free him.
note: One report calls Isaac the sacrificed one; another has Joseph rebuke the keeper and threaten him with the Fire's mountains.

view: The prisoners said they loved Joseph; he begged them not to, recalling that his aunt's love led to an accusation, his father's to the well, and the Aziz's wife's to prison, but they persisted.
note: Some versions omit the aunt or address the prison keeper as well as the two men; one says Joseph desired only his Lord's love.

view: The prisoners invented dreams to test Joseph after he announced or demonstrated that he could interpret dreams; neither had seen what he claimed.
note: Some reports attribute the test to one prisoner's suggestion.

view: Both men actually dreamed, were troubled or curious, and asked Joseph for interpretation; their later interpretations came true.
note: This conflicts with accounts that the dreams were fabricated.

view: Only the baker, who was crucified, lied about his dream; the cupbearer told the truth.
note: This differs from both the two-real-dreams and two-fabricated-dreams reports.

view: After Joseph interpreted the dreams, the men claimed they had only been joking and had not dreamed; Joseph replied that the matter they asked about had been settled.
The phrase 'I see myself' recounts a past dream, even without explicitly saying 'in sleep'; its wording and the later request for interpretation distinguish it from waking action.
note: Some say bare 'I press' would have sufficed for a waking action.

view: The first 'he said' begins an independent clause, since the speech did not occur while entering prison; 'indeed I' is its quoted object.
The perception verb allows subject and object pronouns to refer to the same dreamer; ordinary verbs would require a separate reflexive expression.
One analysis treats arānī as a cognition verb with 'I squeeze' as its second object; another treats 'I squeeze' as a circumstantial clause. Adding a causative hamza would allow a third object.
ʿAṣr means squeezing a moist substance to extract its liquid; ʿaṣīr or ʿuṣāra is the extracted juice. Related usage describes rain pressed from clouds or the arrival of a rainy time.
note: ʿItaṣara can mean having someone else do the squeezing.

view: The cupbearer pressed grapes; khamr can directly mean grapes, including in Omani, Azd, or Ghassan speech and, according to one report, usage known to Quraysh.
note: Al-Dahhak says the Qur'an came in the tongues of different Arab groups.

view: Grapes are called wine in anticipation of the product they will become; Arabic can name a present source by its future result, as with clay called bricks or juice called molasses.
note: This explains the wording differently from treating khamr as the dialect word for grapes.

view: An omitted noun or genitive relation gives the sense 'I press grapes intended for wine' or 'wine grapes.'
note: Al-Qurtubi also gives the related forms khamra, khamr, and khumūr.

view: The object can be called wine itself because the grapes are pressed for wine's sake, as Arabic says 'press oil' while meaning olives.
note: This differs from the claim that khamr directly names grapes.

view: An Arab carrying grapes answered that he carried khamr, illustrating the use of wine for grapes; vinegar made from grapes could likewise be called wine vinegar by association.
Ibn Masud, and in some accounts Ubayy, read 'I press grapes' in place of 'I press wine'; a report says Ibn Masud swore he received this wording from the Prophet.
note: Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, and al-Alusi treat the grapes wording as explanatory gloss rather than canonical recitation.

view: The cupbearer's dream showed three clusters on a vine or in a garden; he pressed their grapes into the king's cup and served him.
note: Versions differ between a grape seed that grew, three branches, and three existing clusters.

view: In Ikrima's fuller account, the dreamer planted a vine, pressed its grapes, and served the king; Joseph predicted he would leave prison in three days and again serve wine.
The wine dream belongs to the king's cupbearer and matches his work; Joseph could infer royal service from the later word 'master.'
The baker dreamed he carried three baskets of bread or assorted food above his head, with birds or birds of prey eating from the top basket.
note: Muqatil also mentions a dish over the three baskets.

view: The bread dream belongs to the baker and reflects his profession: he carried bread while birds ate from it.
note: Al-Biqaʿi glosses carrying as supported lifting for transport and bread as prepared food.

view: In the baker's dream, 'above my head' means on the head or uppermost part; comparisons are made to Qur'anic uses of 'above.'
The bread may have been tharīd; Ibn Masud's codex says tharīd above his head, which Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi treat as an explanatory gloss rather than a recited variant.
Bread is a baked portion of flour and water, also called a loaf.
Al-ṭayr is a feminine collective noun whose singular is ṭāʾir; some also allow ṭayr for one bird, with ṭuyūr as its plural.
'Birds eat from it' qualifies the bread; 'above' can attach to 'I carry' or stand as a circumstantial phrase describing the bread.
Taʾwīl is interpretation: the end, outcome, or reality to which a matter returns; the youths ask what their dreams signify and how their results will unfold.
note: Mujahid also glosses it as telling about the dream itself.

view: The singular pronoun refers to all that the men recounted, like 'that,' or to each man's own dream or to the class of dreams.
note: The notes offer these as alternative antecedents.

view: The plural request recounts what each dreamer may have asked separately; repeating 'he said' for the second prisoner avoids repeating the request.
Their request for an interpretation itself indicates a dream, because an ordinary waking sight needs no dream interpretation.
They praised Joseph for treating prisoners well through care, courtesy, comfort, and practical help; his conduct made him trustworthy to interpret for them.
note: Al-Tabari prefers practical kindness; other notes prefer knowledge or a conditional request.

view: They meant Joseph was accomplished in knowledge or especially skilled at interpreting dreams; ihsān here can mean doing something precisely and well.
note: Ibn al-Anbari supplies an omitted object, 'in knowledge'; Ibn ʿĀshūr says they inferred skill from intelligence without direct proof.

view: Calling Joseph a benefactor is a polite appeal: they promise to count interpretation as a kindness to them, or approach him through his established generosity.
note: Unlike the prior-kindness and skill readings, this praise is conditional on Joseph's response.

view: Joseph is good to himself by obeying God, or he accepts excuses and puts others' rights first; these are offered as additional senses of his excellence.
The men saw signs of Joseph's goodness and assumed that a pure heart perceives events soundly; another account says they had seen him interpret other prisoners' dreams.
A muhsin acts in every matter as if standing in God's presence.
God made Joseph's skill and kindness in prison a path to release: interpreting the two inmates' dreams later led to the king's dream and Joseph's rise.
note: Al-Qushayri emphasizes that companionship can bear fruit after delay, despite the cellmate forgetting Joseph.

view: Joseph's apparently humiliating imprisonment became a source of honor and relief under God's direction; the story repeatedly joins hardship to benefit.
note: Asad relates this to the Qur'anic point that people may dislike what benefits them.

view: Dream interpretation recurs through Jacob's explanation of Joseph's dream, Joseph's own and his companions' dreams, the king's dream, and God-taught waking predictions.
True dreams exist and may disclose future events; denying every true dream conflicts with scripture and prophetic reports. Clear dreams can correspond to later events without needing interpretation.
note: Natural explanations of some dreams do not establish that all dreams are unreal.

view: A Prophetic report says the truest dreams belong to those most truthful in speech.
note: Al-Qurtubi calls the report sahih.

view: Prophetic reports describe a righteous person's dream as a fraction of prophecy: one report says one-fortieth, another one-forty-sixth.
note: The fractions differ in these notes.

view: A Prophetic report divides dreams into self-talk, satanic dreams, and true dreams; al-Razi considers this a rationally sound classification.
A person who falsely claims a dream will be ordered to tie barley grains together on Judgment Day, which cannot be done.
note: Ibn Abbas's report specifies two grains and is graded hasan sahih; Ali's mentions a grain and is graded hasan.

view: The same prophetic report warns that secretly listening to unwilling people's conversation will bring molten lead poured into the listener's ear.
Dream interpretation can disclose reality because the sleeping rational soul is less occupied with the body and encounters higher realities, which appear as images requiring an interpreter.

Ordinary dreams can arise from imagination recombining stored images under bodily conditions, temperament, emotions, chance, or preoccupations; these dreams need not foretell external events, though they still have causes.
True dreams have a real relation to external or hidden events beyond ordinary bodily and emotional causes; the sleeping soul may connect to causes beyond the physical world.

The proposed account distinguishes changing physical matter, an imaginal world of immaterial forms that causes physical events, and an intellectual realm of universal truths that causes the imaginal realm.

A soul may grasp universal causes directly or picture them through familiar images; sound clear dreams perceive causes without distortion, while symbolic dreams use images or opposites and require interpretation.
note: Examples are a crown for honor and darkness for ignorance.

view: Symbolic dreams range from manageable transformations to tangled sequences; the latter are confused dreams that resist interpretation, unlike clear or interpretable symbolic dreams.
Ibn Sirin interpreted sealing people's mouths and sexual organs with a ring as becoming a Ramadan caller whose call to prayer makes people fast.
The cupbearer represents spiritual love; his dream is the wine of love pressed from the heart's knowledge while true witnessing sleeps.

words: أَحْمِلُ فَوْقَ رَأْسِى خُبْزًۭا تَأْكُلُ ٱلطَّيْرُ مِنْهُ
view: The baker represents soul-desire; carrying food for quickly descending birds signifies a total pursuit of pleasure and appetites.
Joseph knew that one prisoner's fate would be painful, so he delayed answering, demonstrated his prophetic knowledge, and called the prisoners to monotheism first.

Before answering, Joseph said he could identify their coming food; most commentators take this as prophetic foreknowledge, while another account says he meant their ordinary waking food, down to what, when, and how much they ate.
note: In the latter account they suspected divination, which Joseph attributed instead to God; al-Tabataba'i finds the dream-food reading less likely.

view: Joseph predicted that the cupbearer would return to service and the baker would be crucified and eaten by birds; the men then denied dreaming.
A scholar asked a question may first offer essential religious counsel and explain relevant knowledge so listeners receive guidance toward God.
note: Al-Tabrisi frames Joseph's address through the call to God's path with wisdom.

view: The two may have told Joseph about their sadness and dreams, or first seen him display dream interpretation; prison inmates commonly discussed dreams and hoped they foretold escape.
Dream interpretation was familiar in Egypt, and the king's later appeal to courtiers shows other people there were thought capable of it; God supported Joseph through this discipline in prison.
The standard recitation ends innī with a short yāʾ; an extended yāʾ is also canonical.
note: The pair occurs in both dreamers' speeches.

view: The standard arānī has a short final yāʾ; an extended yāʾ is also canonical.
note: The pair occurs in both dreamers' speeches.

view: The standard reading retains the hamza in raʾsī; another canonical reading elides it, as classical Arabic permits.
The standard reading retains the hamza in nabbiʾnā; another canonical form elides it without changing the meaning.
note: Al-Nahhas discusses retention of yāʾ in the hamzated form unless the hamza is lightened or replaced.

view: A repeated statement of disbelief in the Hereafter may be emphasis, or the first pronoun can be redundant while the later clause supplies the sentence; another Quranic construction is compared.
note: These notes extend beyond the wording of 12:36.

view: Ḥīn can denote an indefinite period or a fixed six-month period, according to Ikrima's reported senses.
note: This note also glosses muhsinīn as learned and reaches beyond 12:36.

view: A report has the jailer tell Joseph he would improve his treatment but could not free him; Joseph rebuked him as among the evil, destined for the Fire's mountains.

In a comparison with the Queen's 'I submitted with Solomon,' 'with' may express following God and His messenger rather than simultaneous entry; she had thought herself religious before her new submission.
note: Al-Alusi elsewhere prefers concurrence as the original sense when possible.

view: In the food servant's dream, birds of prey pecked at the bread above his head.
The dreamers asked Joseph for interpretation because they regarded him as a benefactor.
